articles.title: Search underway for 1,300 missing after deadly Nepal-Tibet floods
articles.description: Rescue teams rushed Thursday to find more than 1,300 people missing on the Nepal-Tibet border in flash floods and landslides that killed at least 165 and swept away entire villages. A terrifying clip of surveillance video from the Chinese side of the frontier shows a massive wall of mud and debris crashing over a building several stories high on Wednesday morning, engulfing it as dozens of people ran for their lives below. The surge swept away buses and cars like they were toys. Many of the missing are foreign tourists, officials said of the disaster, which the US Geological Survey believes was caused by a glacial collapse that sent a flow of debris engulfing areas along the way. The tsunami-like rumble of water and mud struck villages and towns on the path of two rivers — Bhote Koshi and Trishuli, with Nepali police saying they had recovered 162 bodies. Another 823 people, including 579 Nepali and foreign tourists, remained out of contact in Nepal, according to the country’s disaster agency. Across the border, Chinese state media said the “mudslide disaster” at the Gyirong Port in Tibet claimed three lives while 558 people, including 260 foreigners, were still missing. Police said they expected the death toll to rise beyond 165. “This will go up, as we have resumed the search and more bodies are expected to be recovered,” police spokesperson Abi Narayan Kafle told Reuters . Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah left by road for Bidur in one of the worst-affected districts of Nuwakot to assess the flood situation, his office said on social media. Raju Bhadel, 56, a businessman in Nuwakot, recounted receiving a call from his brother-in-law in distress. “They were crying and said their entire house had been swept away. Three family members were rescued, but his brother is still missing,” he said. Also at Nuwakot, teacher Manok Mishra witnessed “nine trucks being swept away by the floods including people”. This frame grab taken from video released by the Armed Police Force of Nepal on August 26, 2026 shows rescue workers carrying a person after massive floods and landslides in Rasuwa. —AFP ‘Inland tsunami’ Rescuers waded through mud and sludge to look for survivors after floodwaters buried the lower floors of multi-storey buildings. Among those hunting for their missing family members was Subash Khatani, who told AFP he was looking for his big brother. “He is among the missing from Rasuwa. That’s why we are out to search for him,” he said. Among the missing tourists from more than two dozen countries, 177 were from India, 63 were from the United States, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 25 from Canada. Others included tourists from Malaysia, the Netherlands, Portugal, South Africa and South Korea, Nepal’s tourism board said. Hiking company Himalayan Glacier told AFP that 47 people from a group, including two children, were missing in Nepal. “Our teams are checking hospitals where victims are coming in,” said the company’s director Sanket Pandey. The sudden rush of mud and debris was “like an inland tsunami, travelling nearly 170 kilometres down the Bhote Koshi valley into Central Nepal”, said environmental historian Ruth Gamble of La Trobe University. “It is a popular route for international tourists travelling from Kathmandu to Lhasa,” she added. “It was a huge gush of mud coming straight towards us,” said Keshav Prasad Baral, a 68-year-old survivor being treated in a Nepali hospital. “As it got closer, it kept rising higher and higher. When I saw it enter our home, I tried to grab my wife’s hand and take her to the terrace. But she was swept away by the mud.” A helicopter ferried him to safety four hours later. “My wife is still somewhere beneath the mud,” he added. “She’s gone.” Another survivor said he saved himself by clinging to a mango tree as he watched the house where he had been working disappear. Rasuwa, in the north of Nepal, was the first district to be affected. But deaths have been reported from seven Nepali districts in total as the floodwaters raged through to Chitwan in the south, on the border with India. “There is devastation everywhere we look,” said Tula Bahadur BK, a health worker in Rasuwa. “The settlements next to the river have been completely swept away. Five of my own relatives are missing.” The Nepali Army was carrying out flights and had rescued scores of people, while others living near the river in danger zones had been told to relocate. China’s leader Xi Jinping said that “the most urgent task is doing everything possible to search for and rescue the missing people”, according to CCTV . Tibet government officials mobilised nearly 800 emergency workers and 150 vehicles as well as sniffer dogs and speed boats to help the rescue efforts, China’s state-run news agency Xinhua said. The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) said it was dispatching emergency supplies including blankets, first aid kits, stretchers and body bags. “Entire villages and market areas have been wiped out,” said David Fisher, the Nepal head of IFRC. The US State Department said it was sending a disaster response adviser and providing assistance of $500,000. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said details on the disaster were scant. “Nepal ... is a developing country,” he said. “It doesn’t have the resources that an event like that would have in Australia, so information is difficult.” UN teams and partners were sending supplies and personnel to support affected Nepali communities, Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said. Glacial collapse The cause of the disaster was not immediately clear in the hours after it occurred early on Wednesday, but the US Geological Survey said it was a glacial collapse that caused seismic activity and the “catastrophic” downstream impacts in Nepal and Tibet. “This event was initially reported as a magnitude 4.4 earthquake,” it said. “Additional analysis of nearby seismic stations, long-period seismic waves, and satellite imagery led to the determination that the seismic event was instead a glacial collapse and debris flow, and that no earthquake had occurred.” Climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risks of glacial lake floods and glacial collapses. Residents look at a street submerged by mud following flash floods and a landslide disaster in Devighat, in Nepal’s Nuwakot district on August 26, 2026. —AFP Qianggong Zhang, head of climate and environmental risks at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), warned of the potential for a second flood. “With a blockage still lodged upstream on the Nepal-China border river, authorities warn a second flood may occur,” he told AFP. Many trekking companies were not running tours during the monsoon season, but there remain significant numbers of travellers, including pilgrims, in the region. Experts cautioned that a lingering blockage in a river could produce an additional flood. Among sites hit by the flood was Syabrubesi, the gateway to the popular trekking areas, as well as by pilgrims travelling to the base of Mount Kailash, a holy site for Buddhists and Hindus. Traffic authorities in Tibet’s Shigatse said roads in the area were “at risk of mudslides and unsafe for passage”. Buddhist spiritual leader the Dalai Lama said that he was praying for all those killed in devastating floods in Nepal and Tibet. “I pray for all those who have lost their lives, and offer my sympathy and heartfelt condolences to the bereaved and to all those affected by this tragedy,” he said in a statement.

articles.title: Country diary: A pocket rocket of rewilding – and a success in the face of opposition | Amy-Jane Beer
articles.description: Asturias, Spain : I visit a farm that is thrilling in its ecological abundance, created in just eight years On a rocky 13-hectare pocket in the foothills of the Picos de Europa, Luke Massey and Katie Stacey are raising children, dogs, cattle, chicken, ducks, geese and eyebrows. In their eight years here, the farm they call Wild Finca has become a mass of scrub, with scattered large trees and dozens of clearings that Luke calls fields, but which look more like tiny irregular glades, riddled with trails and hemmed all around by the blackthorn, gorse and bramble that has sprung up around the tumbled remains of drystone walls. If Wild Finca is a forever home to the Massey-Staceys, it is a whole world to nature. Witness the butterflies and wasp spiders, the snakes, lizards, hedgehogs and sparrows, and the thousand-piece cricket orchestra that performs each evening as the glow-worms light up. It offers denning and roosting sites for foxes, pine martens, badgers and 17 species of bat, feeding opportunities for roe deer and wild boar, several species of eagle and vulture, and a pit stop for others such as the nightingale I heard singing in early morning mist. articles.title: NIPSCO filed application for customer rate increases amid storm that ravaged Northwest Indiana
articles.description:
Following a devastating derecho that ravaged Northwest Indiana and left hundreds of thousands without power for two weeks, the Northern Indiana Public Service Company filed documents that would raise electric bills for its customers.

NIPSCO filed one rate increase application on Aug. 11 — the day of the storms — and two more on Aug. 14 and 20, respectively, with the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission.

Together, the totals would amount to a nearly $88 annual increase, and at least partially go into effect as soon as Nov. 1 if approved by state regulators, according to documents filed with the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission.

In a statement to the Sun-Times Tuesday, NIPSCO said it was “routine” for it to file the requests. In Indiana, utilities can adjust rates biannually or quarterly for certain types of costs.

The company said it was seeking to “recover” costs for fuel, “regional transmission organization” and “resource adequacy and reliability,” according to filings with the state. Its adjustment for fuel costs asks to “remain in place until replaced by a different fuel cost adjustment that is approved in a subsequent filing.”

But advocates say the company is out of line, as two weeks after the area was stricken with flooding and 99 mph winds, about 100 customers still remained without power Tuesday evening. The total was down from more than 9,300 on Monday. Initially, nearly 60% of its 500,000 customers were without electricity as 335 damaged poles needed to be repaired or replaced and 27 substations required work.

The requests come after a rate hike last year that saw an average NIPSCO customer bill increase 16.75% in July 2025, or nearly $280 a year, which followed an increase in 2024. The Indiana utility regulation agency’s annual bill survey shows that in 2026, the average NIPSCO customer currently pays more than any other Indiana energy customer across all levels of use.

A recent class-action lawsuit representing several Northwest Indiana residents who were affected during the storm also alleges the utility didn’t protect its power lines from “hazardous trees and other vegetation” near power lines despite customer complaints.

Indiana Gov. Mike Braun also called for an investigation into the utility company Monday to “determine whether NIPSCO did what it promised ratepayers and regulators it would do with the money it was given.” He directed the Indiana Office of Utility Consumer Counselor to file a complaint against NIPSCO with the very agency set to hear its case for increasing bills again.

“NIPSCO is a monopoly utility that Hoosiers pay every month with the expectation that it will use its considerable resources to maintain its system, prepare for severe weather and restore service as quickly as possible when disaster strikes,” Braun said in a statement Sunday. “NIPSCO has failed to keep its end of the bargain.”

The requests have yet to be ruled on by Indiana's utility board, and utility companies in Illinois have faced pushback for seeking to increase rates. Earlier this year, Peoples Gas proposed a $202 million rate hike, which would bump gas bills by an average of $130 per year.

But the Illinois attorney general’s office suggested a $4.1 million decrease instead, listing at least $97.2 million in “unsupported and unexplained” cost increases for the company’s pipe retirement program, among other “unsubstantiated” charges.

articles.title: Burkina Faso | Heat waves - Simplified Early Action Protocol Annual Report (MDRBF020), February 15, 2025
articles.description: Country: Burkina Faso Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies Please refer to the attached file. SUMMARY OF THE SIMPLIFIED EARLY ACTION PROTOCOL The IFRC Disaster Response Emergency Fund (DREF) has allocated CHF 219,935 to implement anticipated actions to reduce and mitigate the impact of heatwaves in the city of Ouagadougou in Burkina Faso. This simplified early action protocol includes an allocation of CHF 81,650 to pre-position stocks and CHF 57,212 conduct annual preparedness activities to implement early actions, if and when the trigger is reached. The first actions to be taken have been previously agreed with the National Society and are described in the simplified early action protocol. This report summarizes the annual preparation and pre-positioning activities carried out during the period from January to December 2025. At the end of the first year of implementation of the heatwave PAP in the city of Ouagadougou, significant progress has been made in terms of preparedness and operational capacities for the protection of vulnerable populations.: MOU signed with ANAM for the provision of alerts on heat waves; Eighty (80) volunteers have been trained on the risks associated with heat waves and the management of people at risk; An operational simulation made it possible to test the alert and intervention mechanisms through community awareness-raising actions, home visits and coordination with technical services; Process underway for the pre-positioning of WASH kits for water storage, food for vulnerable people working under the sun, specific products for people with albinism, medical products (blood pressure monitors, thermometers), as well as solar lighting kits for school girls. These kits will be distributed if the trigger is reached; A contract is being signed with ONEA for the supply of drinking water in cisterns in the event of an alert; A framework contract is being signed with a private service provider for the rental of tanks in the event of a trip; Participatory targeting identified the most at-risk groups, including people living in undeveloped areas, the elderly, people living with disabilities, people with albinism or leprosy; A 2026-2027 heatwave response action plan has been developed to enable the CRBF to be more operational in the event that triggers are reached throughout the country. These actions have contributed to strengthening the capacity of the National Society and improving coordination with national actors involved in climate risk management.

articles.title: Malawi | Pluvial Floods: Simplified Early Action Protocol - Operations Update (MDRMW023), 30th April 2026
articles.description: Country: Malawi Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies Please refer to the attached file. SIMPLIFIED EARLY ACTION PROTOCOL Situation Overview Following the issuance of the forecast by the Department of Climate Change and Meteorological Services (DCCMS) on 6 January 2026, the Malawi Red Cross Society (MRCS) activated its sEAP in line with the impact-based forecast dataset generated by DCCMS, targeting selected areas in the Central Region and parts of the lakeshore districts. Based on the technical guidance provided, Salima District was prioritised for implementation of Early Actions. This decision was informed by the trigger thresholds outlined in the sEAP and observed water level trends, which indicated a high risk of flooding. By 8 January, prior to the onset of heavy rains, pre-targeting of vulnerable households and beneficiaries was conducted in close coordination with Salima District Council stakeholders, particularly the District Disaster Risk Management Office and the Social Welfare Office. In addition, MRCS undertook community alert and preparedness activities aimed at enhancing awareness, reducing risks, and safeguarding lives and livelihoods.

articles.title: Lao PDR: Lao People's Democratic Republic: Flood 2026 - DREF Operation (MDRLA012)
articles.description: Country: Lao People's Democratic Republic (the) Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies Please refer to the attached file. Description of the Event Date of event 14-08-2026 What happened, where and when? Since late June 2026, Lao PDR has experienced recurrent flooding, flash floods, waterlogging and landslides associated with the southwest monsoon, Tropical Storm Maysak and subsequent weather systems. While flooding was first reported in late June, the situation progressively worsened through July and August as prolonged and repeated heavy rainfall caused cumulative impacts, with already affected areas experiencing further flooding, waterlogging and landslides, increasing damage and disrupting access. By August, the scale and persistence of the emergency had exceeded Lao Red Cross (LRC)'s available resources and response capacity, leading LRC to determine on 14 August 2026 that additional resources through the DREF were required to sustain and scale up the response. According to UN site rep report release in July and August 2026, prolonged heavy rainfall caused flooding in several parts of Lao PDR. On 4 July, a wooden bridge was swept away in Vang Vieng, Vientiane Province, and a road was disrupted in Sepon District, Savannakhet Province. In Khammouane Province, flooding affected multiple districts, including Nakai, Khounkham and Xaybouathong, between 8 and 13 July, damaging houses, agricultural land and infrastructure. On 16 to 17 July, a landslide in Thabak Village, Khamkeut District, Bolikhamxay Province, resulted in three fatalities. On 21 July, severe flooding was reported in Khounkham District, Khammouane Province. Further rainfall in late July caused flash flooding in Nasangveuy Village, Luang Prabang Province, and persistent waterlogging in parts of Sikhottabong District, Vientiane Capital. At the end of the month, heavy rainfall damaged the road connecting Luang Prabang and Houaphanh provinces, disrupting transportation and leaving vehicles stranded. During early August 2026, heavy rainfall continued to cause flooding and access disruptions across several parts of Lao PDR. On 3 August, severe flash flooding was reported in Luang Prabang Province. On 4 August, the Xe Champhone River in Champhone District, Savannakhet Province, exceeded the warning level, reaching 8.02 metres. On 5 August, flood warnings were issued for the Nam Xan, Nam Xebangfai and Nam Tha river basins as water levels continued to rise. During the same period, heavy rainfall and erosion disrupted road access in Khounkham District, Khammouane Province, including the Phou Phaman road section and parts of Route 8A. Further flooding was reported on 9 to 10 August in several affected areas, prompting assessments by Lao Red Cross branches. By mid-August, flood incidents had been reported across six provinces: Khammouane, Savannakhet, Bolikhamxay, Luang Namtha, Xiengkhouang and Champasak. As of 17 August, LRC at headquarters consolidated the assessments from its branches, flooding had affected 25 districts and 395 villages, 22,390 households, approximately 114,037 people across these provinces (Khammouan, Xiengkhouang, Bolikhamxay, Louang Namtha, Savannakhet, Champasak) causing damage to agricultural land, housing, roads and access to basic services. The latest UN Lao PDR Monsoon Situation Report No. 3, dated 19 August 2026, confirms that the situation continued to intensify during August, most recently, on 19 August, flash flooding struck Nan District, Luang Prabang Province, as heavy rainfall over several consecutive hours combined forest runoff with rising waters of the Nam Nan River, flooding homes and agricultural land along the riverbank; the same morning, a sudden flash flood at 3:30 AM struck Huay La Village, Beng District, Oudomxay Province, causing severe property damage to many families. The forecast indicates an increased risk of flooding, flash floods and landslides, particularly in northern and central Lao PDR during 18-21 August 2026. Flooding was reported across several provinces, and LRC initially responded using its own available resources, including the mobilisation of provincial branches, volunteers and pre-positioned relief items. At the same time, LRC conducted rapid assessments to monitor the evolving situation, identify affected populations and determine priority needs. As the flooding became cumulative and recurrent, with continued heavy rainfall and worsening conditions in several affected areas, humanitarian needs increased beyond the capacity of affected households and local response mechanisms to cope. Government authorities activated disaster management structures and supported evacuation, emergency relief and restoration of access, while LRC continued to mobilise provincial resources, distribute emergency relief items and provide safe water. However, the assessment findings and continued monitoring indicated that the scale and persistence of the needs were exceeding LRC's available resources and response capacity. Significant gaps remained in essential assistance, particularly as the situation continued to evolve and additional communities were affected. LRC determined on 14 August 2026 that additional resources were required to sustain and scale up its response. Therefore, LRC formally decided that DREF support was necessary, rather than the initial onset of flooding.
